verses.zh: 耶稣被圣灵充满，从约旦河回来，圣灵将他引到旷野，四十天受魔鬼的试探。
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan River[NOTE:2] and was led by the Spirit[NOTE:3] in[NOTE:4] the wilderness,[NOTE:5]
notes: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “then” to indicate continuity with the previous topic.
“River” is not in the Greek text but is supplied for clarity.
The double mention of the Spirit in this verse makes it clear that the temptation was neither the fault of Jesus nor an accident.

Most mss (A Θ Ξ Ψ 0102 ƒ1,13 33 M lat) read εἰς τὴν ἔρημον (eis tēn erēmon, “into the wilderness”), apparently motivated by the parallel in Matt 4:1. However, the reading behind the translation (ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ, en tē erēmō) is found in overall better witnesses (P4vid,7, 75vid א B D L W 579 892 1241 it).

Or “desert.”sn The Judean Wilderness (or Judean Desert) is a geographical feature extending from the mountains of Judea in the west to the Dead Sea in the east. It is a relatively small desert, covering only about 600 square miles (roughly 1,500 square km). The Judean Wilderness is characterized by breathtaking panoramas: mountains, cliffs, chalk hills, and plateaus are interrupted by riverbeds and canyons, some of which are up to 1,500 feet (500 m) deep. Some of the rivers are seasonal streams and some have water all year round. The tall cliffs on the eastern edge of the desert reach a height of 1,000 feet (300 m) above the shore of the Dead Sea. The Judean Wilderness is close to Jerusalem and sparsely populated with few settlements around its edges. It is known for its rugged and desolate landscape, which has provided a refuge and hiding place for rebels and zealots throughout history, as well as solitude for monks and hermits.

verses.zh: 那些日子没有吃甚么；日子满了，他就饿了。
verses.en: where for forty days he endured temptations[NOTE:1] from the devil. He[NOTE:2] ate nothing[NOTE:3] during those days, and when they were completed,[NOTE:4] he was famished.
notes: Grk “in the desert, for forty days being tempted.” The participle πειραζόμενος (peirazomenos) has been translated as an adverbial clause in English to avoid a run-on sentence with a second “and.” Here the present participle suggests a period of forty days of testing. Three samples of the end of the testing are given in the following verses.
Grk “And he.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.

The reference to Jesus eating nothing could well be an idiom meaning that he ate only what the desert provided; see Exod 34:28. A desert fast simply meant eating only what one could obtain in the desert. The parallel in Matt 4:2 speaks only of Jesus fasting.

This verb and its cognate noun, sunteleia, usually implies not just the end of an event, but its completion or fulfillment. The noun is always used in the NT in eschatological contexts; the verb is often so used (cf. Matt 13:39, 40; 24:3; 28:20; Mark 13:4; Rom 9:28; Heb 8:8; 9:26). The idea here may be that the forty-day period of temptation was designed for a particular purpose in the life of Christ (the same verb is used in v. 13). The cognate verb teleioō is a key NT term for the completion of God’s plan: See Luke 12:50; 22:37; John 19:30; and (where it has the additional component of meaning “to perfect”) Heb 2:10; 5:8-9; 7:28.tn The Greek word here is συντελεσθείσων (suntelestheisōn) from the verb συντελέω (sunteleō).

verses.zh: 魔鬼对他说：「你若是　神的儿子，可以吩咐这块石头变成食物。」
verses.en: The devil said to him, “If[NOTE:1] you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread.”[NOTE:2]
notes: This is a first class condition: “If (and let’s assume that you are) the Son of God…”
Grk “say to this stone that it should become bread.”

verses.zh: 耶稣回答说：「经上记着说：『人活着不是单靠食物，乃是靠　神口里所出的一切话。』」
verses.en: Jesus answered him, “It is written, ‘Man[NOTE:1] does not live by bread alone.’”[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “a person.” The Greek word ὁ ἄνθρωπος (ho anthrōpos) is used generically for humanity. The translation “man” is used because the emphasis in Jesus’ response seems to be on his dependence on God as a man.

A quotation from Deut 8:3. Jesus will live by doing God’s will, and will take no shortcuts. tc Most mss (A [D] Θ Ψ [0102] ƒ1,13 33 M latt) complete the citation with ἀλλ᾿ ἐπὶ παντὶ ῥήματι θεοῦ (all’ epi panti rhēmati theou, “but by every word from God”), an assimilation to Matt 4:4 (which is a quotation of Deut 8:3). The shorter reading is found in א B L W 1241 sa. There is no good reason why scribes would omit the rest of the quotation here. The shorter reading, on both internal and external grounds, should be considered the autographic wording in Luke.

verses.zh: 魔鬼又领他上了高山，霎时间把天下的万国都指给他看，
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] the devil[NOTE:2] led him up[NOTE:3] to a high place[NOTE:4] and showed him in a flash all the kingdoms of the world.
notes: The order of Luke’s temptations differs from Matthew’s at this point as numbers two and three are reversed. It is slightly more likely that Luke has made the change to put the Jerusalem temptation last, as Jerusalem is so important to Luke’s later account. The temporal markers in Matthew’s account are also slightly more specific.tn Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Grk “he.”

Most mss (א1 A [D W] Θ Ψ 0102 ƒ1,[13] 33 700 2542 M it) refer to Jesus being taken up “to a high mountain” (with many of these also explicitly adding “the devil”) here in parallel with Matt 4:8, but both scribal harmonization to that text and the pedigree of the witnesses for the shorter reading (א* B L 1241) is the reason it should be omitted from Luke.
“A high place” is not in the Greek text but has been supplied for clarity.

verses.zh: 对他说：「这一切权柄、荣华，我都要给你，因为这原是交付我的，我愿意给谁就给谁。
verses.en: And he[NOTE:1] said to him, “To you[NOTE:2] I will grant this whole realm[NOTE:3]—and the glory that goes along with it,[NOTE:4] for it has been relinquished[NOTE:5] to me, and I can give it to anyone I wish.
notes: Grk “And the devil.”
In Greek, this phrase is in an emphatic position. In effect, the devil is tempting Jesus by saying, “Look what you can have!”
Or “authority.” BDAG 353 s.v. ἐξουσία 6 suggests, concerning this passage, that the term means “the sphere in which the power is exercised, domain.” Cf. also Luke 22:53; 23:7; Acts 26:18; Eph 2:2.
The addendum referring to the glory of the kingdoms of the world forms something of an afterthought, as the following pronoun (“it”) makes clear, for the singular refers to the realm itself.
For the translation of παραδέδοται (paradedotai) see L&N 57.77. The devil is erroneously implying that God has given him such authority with the additional capability of sharing the honor.

verses.zh: 你若在我面前下拜，这都要归你。」
verses.en: So then, if[NOTE:1] you will worship[NOTE:2] me, all this will be[NOTE:3] yours.”
notes: This is a third class condition: “If you worship me (and I am not saying whether you will or will not)…”
Or “will prostrate yourself in worship before…” The verb προσκυνέω (proskuneō) can allude not only to the act of worship but the position of the worshiper. See L&N 53.56.
One could translate this phrase “it will all be yours.” The sense is the same, but the translation given is a touch more emphatic and more likely to catch the force of the offer.

verses.zh: 耶稣说：「经上记着说：当拜主―你的　神，单要事奉他。」
verses.en: Jesus[NOTE:1] answered him,[NOTE:2] “It is written, ‘You are to worship[NOTE:3] the Lord[NOTE:4] your God and serve only him.’”[NOTE:5]
notes: Grk “And Jesus.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.

Most mss, especially the later ones (A Θ Ψ 0102 ƒ13 M it), have “Get behind me, Satan!” at the beginning of the quotation. This roughly parallels Matt 4:10 (though the Lukan mss add ὀπίσω μου to read ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μου, σατανᾶ [hupage opisō mou, satana]); for this reason the words are suspect as a later addition to make the two accounts agree more precisely. A similar situation occurred in v. 5.
Or “You will prostrate yourself in worship before…” The verb προσκυνέω (proskuneō) can allude not only to the act of worship but the position of the worshiper. See L&N 53.56.

Most later mss (A Θ 0102 M) alter the word order by moving the verb forward in the quotation. This alteration removes the emphasis from “the Lord your God” as the one to receive worship (as opposed to Satan) by moving it away from the beginning of the quotation.sn In the form of the quotation in the Greek text found in the best mss, it is the unique sovereignty of the Lord that has the emphatic position.
A quotation from Deut 6:13. The word “only” is an interpretive expansion not found in either the Hebrew or Greek (LXX) text of the OT.

verses.zh: 魔鬼又领他到耶路撒冷去，叫他站在殿顶（顶：原文是翅）上，对他说：「你若是　神的儿子，可以从这里跳下去；
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] the devil[NOTE:2] brought him to Jerusalem,[NOTE:3] had him stand[NOTE:4] on the highest point of the temple,[NOTE:5] and said to him, “If[NOTE:6] you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here,
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Grk “he”; the referent (the devil) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
Grk “and stood him.”

What the highest point of the temple refers to is unclear. Perhaps the most popular suggestion is that the word refers to the point on the temple’s southeast corner where it looms directly over a cliff some 450 ft (135 m) high. Others have suggested the reference could be to the roof of the temple or a projection of the roof; still others see a reference to the lintel of the temple’s high gate, or a tower in the temple courts. The Greek word itself could be literally translated “winglet” (a diminutive of the Greek word for “wing”) which may have been chosen as a wordplay on the reference to safety under the “wings” of God in Ps 91:4, the same psalm quoted by the devil in the following verse.
This is another first class condition, as in v. 3.

verses.zh: 因为经上记着说：主要为你吩咐他的使者保护你；
verses.en: for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you, to protect you,’[NOTE:1]
notes: A quotation from Ps 91:11 by the devil. This was not so much an incorrect citation as a use in a wrong context (a misapplication of the passage).

verses.zh: 他们要用手托着你，免得你的脚碰在石头上。」
verses.en: and ‘with their hands they will lift you up, so that you will not strike your foot against a stone.’”[NOTE:1]
notes: A quotation from Ps 91:12.

verses.zh: 耶稣对他说：「经上说：『不可试探主―你的　神。』」
verses.en: Jesus[NOTE:1] answered him,[NOTE:2] “It is said, ‘You are not to put the Lord your God to the test.’”[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “And Jesus.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “Jesus, answering, said to him.” This is redundant in English and has been simplified to “Jesus answered him.”
A quotation from Deut 6:16 used by Jesus in reply to the devil. The point is that God’s faithfulness should not be put to the test, but is rather a given.

verses.zh: 魔鬼用完了各样的试探，就暂时离开耶稣。
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] when the devil[NOTE:2] had completed every temptation, he departed from him until a more opportune time.[NOTE:3]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate a summary.
Grk “he”; the referent (the devil) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Until a more opportune time. Though some have argued that the devil disappears until Luke 22:3, this is unlikely since the cosmic battle with Satan and all the evil angels is consistently mentioned throughout Luke (8:26-39; 11:14-23).tn Grk “until a favorable time.”

verses.zh: 耶稣满有圣灵的能力，回到加利利；他的名声就传遍了四方。
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] Jesus, in the power of the Spirit,[NOTE:2] returned to Galilee, and news about him spread[NOTE:3] throughout the surrounding countryside.[NOTE:4]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Once again Jesus is directed by the Spirit. Luke makes a point about Jesus’ association with the Spirit early in his ministry (3:22; 4:1 [2x]; 4:18).
Grk “went out.”
Grk “all the surrounding region.”

verses.zh: 他在各会堂里教训人，众人都称赞他。
verses.en: He[NOTE:1] began to teach[NOTE:2] in their synagogues[NOTE:3] and was praised[NOTE:4] by all.
notes: Grk “And he.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
The imperfect verb has been translated ingressively.

The next incident in Luke 4:16-30 is probably to be seen as an example of this ministry of teaching in their synagogues in Galilee. Synagogues were places for Jewish prayer and worship, with recognized leadership (cf. Luke 8:41). Though the origin of the synagogue is not entirely clear, it seems to have arisen in the postexilic community during the intertestamental period. A town could establish a synagogue if there were at least ten men. In normative Judaism of the NT period, the OT scripture was read and discussed in the synagogue by the men who were present (see the Mishnah, m. Megillah 3-4; m. Berakhot 2).

Grk “being glorified.” The participle δοξαζόμενος (doxazomenos) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style. This is the only place Luke uses the verb δοξάζω (doxazō) of Jesus.

verses.zh: 耶稣来到拿撒勒，就是他长大的地方。在安息日，照他平常的规矩进了会堂，站起来要念圣经。
verses.en: Now[NOTE:1] Jesus[NOTE:2] came to Nazareth,[NOTE:3] where he had been brought up, and went into the synagogue[NOTE:4] on the Sabbath day, as was his custom.[NOTE:5] He[NOTE:6] stood up to read,[NOTE:7]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “now” to indicate the transition to a new topic.
Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
For location see Map1-D3; Map2-C2; Map3-D5; Map4-C1; Map5-G3.sn Nazareth was Jesus’ hometown (which is why he is known as Jesus of Nazareth) about 20 miles (30 km) southwest from Capernaum.
See the note on synagogues in 4:15.
Grk “according to his custom.”
Grk “And he.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.

In normative Judaism of the period, the OT scripture was read and discussed in the synagogue by the men who were present. See the Mishnah, m. Megillah 3-4; m. Berakhot 2. First came the law, then the prophets, then someone was asked to speak on the texts. Normally one stood up to read out of respect for the scriptures, and then sat down (v. 20) to expound them.

verses.zh: 有人把先知以赛亚的书交给他，他就打开，找到一处写着说：
verses.en: and the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He[NOTE:1] unrolled[NOTE:2] the scroll and found the place where it was written,
notes: Grk “And unrolling the scroll he found.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style. Instead a new sentence has been started in the translation.
Grk “opening,” but a scroll of this period would have to be unrolled. The participle ἀναπτύξας (anaptuxas) has been translated as a finite verb due to the requirements of contemporary English style.

verses.zh: 主的灵在我身上，因为他用膏膏我，叫我传福音给贫穷的人；差遣我报告：被掳的得释放，瞎眼的得看见，叫那受压制的得自由，
verses.en: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed[NOTE:1] me to proclaim good news[NOTE:2] to the poor.[NOTE:3] He has sent me[NOTE:4] to proclaim release[NOTE:5] to the captives and the regaining of sight[NOTE:6] to the blind,to set free[NOTE:7] those who are oppressed,[NOTE:8]
notes: The phrase he has anointed me is an allusion back to Jesus’ baptism in Luke 3:21-22.
Grk “to evangelize,” “to preach the gospel.”

The poor is a key term in Luke. It refers to the pious poor and indicates Jesus’ desire to reach out to those the world tends to forget or mistreat. It is like 1:52 in force and also will be echoed in 6:20 (also 1 Pet 2:11-25). Jesus is commissioned to do this.

The majority of mss, especially the later Byzantines, include the phrase “to heal the brokenhearted” at this point (A Θ Ψ 0102 ƒ1 M). The phrase is lacking in several weighty mss (א B D L W Ξ ƒ13 33 579 700 892* lat sys co), including representatives from both the Alexandrian and Western text-forms. From the standpoint of external evidence, the omission of the phrase is more likely what the initial text read. When internal evidence is considered, the shorter reading becomes almost certain. Scribes would be much more prone to add the phrase here to align the text with Isa 61:1, the source of the quotation, than to remove it from the initial text.
The release in view here is comprehensive, both at a physical level and a spiritual one, as the entire ministry of Jesus makes clear (Luke 1:77-79; 7:47; 24:47; Acts 2:38; 5:31; 10:43).
Again, as with the previous phrase, regaining of sight may well mean more than simply miraculously restoring physical sight, which itself pictures a deeper reality (Luke 1:77-79; 18:35-43).

The essence of Jesus’ messianic work is expressed in the phrase to set free. This line from Isa 58 says that Jesus will do what the nation had failed to do. It makes the proclamation messianic, not merely prophetic, because Jesus doesn’t just proclaim the message—he brings the deliverance. The word translated set free is the same Greek word (ἄφεσις, aphesis) translated release earlier in the verse.
Again, as with the previous phrases, oppressed may well mean more than simply political or economic oppression, but a deeper reality of oppression by sin (Luke 1:77-79; 18:35-43).

verses.zh: 报告　神悦纳人的禧年。
verses.en: to proclaim the year[NOTE:1] of the Lord’s favor.”[NOTE:2]
notes: The year of the Lord’s favor (Grk “the acceptable year of the Lord”) is a description of the Year of Jubilee (Lev 25:10). The year of the total forgiveness of debt is now turned into a metaphor for salvation. Jesus had come to proclaim that God was ready to forgive sin totally.
A quotation from Isa 61:1-2a. Within the citation is a line from Isa 58:6, with its reference to setting the oppressed free.

verses.zh: 于是把书卷起来，交还执事，就坐下。会堂里的人都定睛看他。
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] he rolled up[NOTE:2] the scroll, gave it back to the attendant, and sat down. The eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed on[NOTE:3] him.
notes: Grk “And closing.” Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the transition to a new topic.
Grk “closing,” but a scroll of this period would have to be rolled up. The participle πτύξας (ptuxas) has been translated as a finite verb due to the requirements of contemporary English style.
Or “gazing at,” “staring at.”

verses.zh: 耶稣对他们说：「今天这经应验在你们耳中了。」
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] he began to tell them, “Today[NOTE:2] this scripture has been fulfilled even as you heard it being read.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
See the note on today in 2:11.
Grk “in your hearing.”

verses.zh: 众人都称赞他，并希奇他口中所出的恩言；又说：「这不是约瑟的儿子吗？」
verses.en: All[NOTE:1] were speaking well of him, and were amazed at the gracious words coming out of his mouth. They[NOTE:2] said, “Isn’t this[NOTE:3] Joseph’s son?”
notes: Grk “And all.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “And they.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.

The form of the question assumes a positive reply. It really amounts to an objection, as Jesus’ response in the next verses shows. Jesus spoke smoothly and impressively. He made a wonderful declaration, but could a local carpenter’s son make such an offer? That was their real question.

verses.zh: 耶稣对他们说：「你们必引这俗语向我说：『医生，你医治自己吧！我们听见你在迦百农所行的事，也当行在你自己家乡里』」；
verses.en: Jesus[NOTE:1] said to them, “No doubt you will quote to me the proverb, ‘Physician, heal yourself!’[NOTE:2] and say, ‘What we have heard that you did in Capernaum,[NOTE:3] do here in your hometown too.’”
notes: Grk “And he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity. Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
The proverb Physician, heal yourself! means that Jesus should prove his claims. It is a “Prove it to us!” mentality that Jesus says the people have.

For location see Map1-D2; Map2-C3; Map3-B2.sn The remark “What we have heard that you did at Capernaum” makes many suspect that Luke has moved this event forward in sequence to typify what Jesus’ ministry was like, since the ministry in Capernaum follows in vv. 31-44. The location of this event in the parallel of Mark 6:1-6 also suggests this transposition. On Capernaum itself, see the note at Luke 4:31.

verses.zh: 又说：「我实在告诉你们，没有先知在自己家乡被人悦纳的。
verses.en: And he added,[NOTE:1] “I tell you the truth,[NOTE:2] no prophet is acceptable[NOTE:3] in his hometown.
notes: Grk “said,” but since this is a continuation of previous remarks, “added” is used here.
Grk “Truly (ἀμήν, amēn), I say to you.”

Jesus argues that he will get no respect in his own hometown. There is a wordplay here on the word acceptable (δεκτός, dektos), which also occurs in v. 19: Jesus has declared the “acceptable” year of the Lord (here translated year of the Lord’s favor), but he is not “accepted” by the people of his own hometown.

verses.zh: 我对你们说实话，当以利亚的时候，天闭塞了三年零六个月，遍地有大饥荒，那时，以色列中有许多寡妇，
verses.en: But in truth I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in Elijah’s days,[NOTE:1] when the sky[NOTE:2] was shut up three and a half years and[NOTE:3] there was a great famine over all the land.
notes: Elijah’s days. Jesus, by discussing Elijah and Elisha, pictures one of the lowest periods in Israel’s history. These examples, along with v. 24, also show that Jesus is making prophetic claims as well as messianic ones. See 1 Kgs 17-18.

Or “the heaven”; the Greek word οὐρανός (ouranos) may be translated “sky” or “heaven,” depending on the context. Since the context here refers to a drought (which produced the famine), “sky” is preferable.
Grk “as.” The particle ὡς can also function temporally (see BDAG 1105-6 s.v. 8).

verses.zh: 以利亚并没有奉差往她们一个人那里去，只奉差往西顿的撒勒法一个寡妇那里去。
verses.en: Yet[NOTE:1] Elijah was sent to none of them, but only to a woman who was a widow at Zarephath in Sidon.[NOTE:2]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “yet” to indicate the contrast.

Zarephath in Sidon was Gentile territory (see 1 Kgs 17:9-24). Jesus’ point was that he would be forced to minister elsewhere, and the implication is that this ministry would ultimately extend (through the work of his followers) to those outside the nation.map For location see Map1-A1; JP3-F3; JP4-F3.

verses.zh: 先知以利沙的时候，以色列中有许多长大麻疯的，但内中除了叙利亚国的乃缦，没有一个得洁净的。」
verses.en: And there were many lepers[NOTE:1] in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha,[NOTE:2] yet[NOTE:3] none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.”[NOTE:4]
notes: The ancient term for leprosy covers a wider array of conditions than what is called leprosy today (Hansen’s disease). In the OT the Hebrew term generally referred to a number of exfoliative (scaly) skin diseases (when applied to humans). A person with one of these diseases was totally ostracized from society until he was declared cured (Lev 13:45-46). In the NT the Greek term also refers to a number of skin diseases, but there is some evidence that true leprosy (Hansen’s disease) could be referred to, since that disease began to be described by Greek physicians in Alexandria, Egypt around 300 B.C. and thus might have been present in Judea and Galilee just before the time of Jesus.
On Elisha see 2 Kgs 5:1-14.
Here καί (kai) has been translated as “yet” to indicate the contrast.

The reference to Naaman the Syrian (see 2 Kgs 5:1-24) is another example where an outsider and Gentile was blessed. The stress in the example is the missed opportunity of the people to experience God’s work, but it will still go on without them.

verses.zh: 会堂里的人听见这话，都怒气满胸，
verses.en: When they heard this, all the people[NOTE:1] in the synagogue were filled with rage.
notes: The words “the people” are not in the Greek text but have been supplied.

verses.zh: 就起来撵他出城（他们的城造在山上）；他们带他到山崖，要把他推下去。
verses.en: They got up, forced[NOTE:1] him out of the town,[NOTE:2] and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, so that[NOTE:3] they could throw him down the cliff.[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “cast.”
Or “city.”
The Greek conjunction ὥστε (hōste) here indicates their purpose.

The attempt to throw him down the cliff looks like “lynch law,” but it may really be an indication that Jesus was regarded as a false prophet who was worthy of death (Deut 13:5). Such a sentence meant being thrown into a pit and then stoned.

verses.zh: 他却从他们中间直行，过去了。
verses.en: But he passed through the crowd[NOTE:1] and went on his way.[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “their midst.”

The verb πορεύομαι (poreuomai) in Luke often suggests divine direction, “to go in a led direction” (4:42; 7:6, 11; 9:51, 52, 56, 57; 13:33; 17:11; 22:22, 29; 24:28). It could suggest that Jesus is on a journey, a theme that definitely is present later in Luke 9-19.

verses.zh: 耶稣下到迦百农，就是加利利的一座城，在安息日教训众人。
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] he went down to Capernaum,[NOTE:2] a town[NOTE:3] in Galilee, and on the Sabbath he began to teach the people.[NOTE:4]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate the continuation of the topic; in light of his rejection at Nazareth, Jesus went on to Capernaum.

For location see Map1-D2; Map2-C3; Map3-B2.sn Capernaum was a town located on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, 680 ft (204 m) below sea level. It existed since Hasmonean times and was a major trade and economic center in the North Galilean region. The population in the first century is estimated to be around 1,500. Capernaum became the hub of operations for Jesus’ Galilean ministry (Matt 4:13; Mark 2:1). In modern times the site was discovered in 1838 by the American explorer E. Robinson, and major excavations began in 1905 by German archaeologists H. Kohl and C. Watzinger. Not until 1968, however, were remains from the time of Jesus visible; in that year V. Corbo and S. Loffreda began a series of annual archaeological campaigns that lasted until 1985. This work uncovered what is thought to be the house of Simon Peter as well as ruins of the first century synagogue beneath the later synagogue from the fourth or fifth century A.D. Today gently rolling hills and date palms frame the first century site, a favorite tourist destination of visitors to the Galilee.
Or “city.”
Grk “them”; the referent (the people) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 他们很希奇他的教训，因为他的话里有权柄。
verses.en: They[NOTE:1] were amazed[NOTE:2] at his teaching because he spoke[NOTE:3] with authority.[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “And they.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
They were amazed. The astonishment shown here is like that in Luke 2:48.
Grk “because his word was.”

Jesus’ teaching impressed the hearers with the directness of its claim (with authority). A study of Jewish rabbinic interpretation shows that it was typical to cite a list of authorities to make one’s point. Apparently Jesus addressed the issues in terms of his own understanding.

verses.zh: 在会堂里有一个人，被污鬼的精气附着，大声喊叫说：
verses.en: Now[NOTE:1] in the synagogue[NOTE:2] there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean[NOTE:3] demon, and he cried out with a loud voice,
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “now” to indicate the transition to a specific example of how Jesus spoke with authority (v. 32).
See the note on synagogues in 4:15.
Grk “having an unclean, demonic spirit,” that is, an evil spirit. This is the only place Luke uses this lengthy phrase. Normally he simply says an “unclean spirit.”

verses.zh: 「唉！拿撒勒的耶稣，我们与你有甚么相干？你来灭我们吗？我知道你是谁，乃是　神的圣者。」
verses.en: “Ha! Leave us alone,[NOTE:1] Jesus the Nazarene! Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One[NOTE:2] of God.”
notes: Grk “What to us and to you?” This is an idiom meaning, “We have nothing to do with one another,” or “Why bother us!” The phrase τί ἡμῖν καὶ σοί (ti hēmin kai soi) is Semitic in origin, though it made its way into colloquial Greek (BDAG 275 s.v. ἐγώ). The equivalent Hebrew expression in the Old Testament had two basic meanings: (1) When one person was unjustly bothering another, the injured party could say “What to me and to you?” meaning, “What have I done to you that you should do this to me?” (Judg 11:12; 2 Chr 35:21; 1 Kgs 17:18). (2) When someone was asked to get involved in a matter he felt was no business of his, he could say to the one asking him, “What to me and to you?” meaning, “That is your business, how am I involved?” (2 Kgs 3:13; Hos 14:8). Option (1) implies hostility, while option (2) merely implies disengagement. BDAG suggests the following as glosses for this expression: What have I to do with you? What have we in common? Leave me alone! Never mind! Hostility between Jesus and the demons is certainly to be understood in this context, hence the translation: “Leave me alone….” For a very similar expression, see Luke 8:28 and (in a different context) John 2:4.

The confession of Jesus as the Holy One here is significant, coming from an unclean spirit. Jesus, as the Holy One of God, who bears God’s Spirit and is the expression of holiness, comes to deal with uncleanness and unholiness.

verses.zh: 耶稣责备他说：「不要作声，从这人身上出来吧！」鬼把那人摔倒在众人中间，就出来了，却也没有害他。
verses.en: But[NOTE:1] Jesus rebuked him:[NOTE:2] “Silence! Come out of him!”[NOTE:3] Then, after the demon threw the man[NOTE:4] down in their midst, he came out of him without hurting him.[NOTE:5]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “but” to indicate the contrast involved in Jesus’ reply.
Grk “rebuked him, saying.” The participle λέγων (legōn) is redundant in English and has not been translated.
The command Come out of him! is an example of Jesus’ authority (see v. 32). Unlike other exorcists, Jesus did not use magical incantations nor did he invoke anyone else’s name.
Grk “him”; the referent (the man) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The departure of the evil spirit from the man without hurting him shows Jesus’ total deliverance and protection of this individual.

verses.zh: 众人都惊讶，彼此对问说：「这是甚么道理呢？因为他用权柄能力吩咐污鬼，污鬼就出来。」
verses.en: They[NOTE:1] were all amazed and began to say[NOTE:2] to one another, “What’s happening here?[NOTE:3] For with authority and power[NOTE:4] he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!”
notes: Grk “And they.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
This imperfect verb has been translated as an ingressive imperfect.
Grk “What is this word?” The Greek term λόγος (logos) has a wide range of meaning. Here it seems to mean, “What is this matter?” More idiomatically it would be, “What’s going on here?!”

The phrase with authority and power is in an emphatic position in the Greek text. Once again the authority of Jesus is the point, but now it is not just his teaching that is emphasized, but his ministry. Jesus combined word and deed into a powerful testimony in Capernaum.

verses.zh: 于是耶稣的名声传遍了周围地方。
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] the news[NOTE:2] about him spread into all areas of the region.[NOTE:3]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate resultative nature of the action.
That is, “information concerning a person or an event—‘report, news, word, information’” (L&N 33.211).
Given Luke 4:31, the phrase the region is a reference to Galilee.

verses.zh: 耶稣出了会堂，进了西门的家。西门的岳母害热病甚重，有人为她求耶稣。
verses.en: After Jesus left[NOTE:1] the synagogue, he entered Simon’s house.[NOTE:2] Now Simon’s mother-in-law was suffering from a high fever, and they asked Jesus[NOTE:3] to help her.[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “Arising from the synagogue, he entered.” The participle ἀναστάς (anastas) has been taken temporally here, and the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

There is now significant agreement among scholars that the house of Simon Peter in Capernaum has been found beneath the ruins of a fifth-century Byzantine church some 84 ft south of the synagogue. At the bottom of several layers of archaeological remains is a first-century house that apparently was designated for public viewing sometime in the mid-first century, and continued to be so in subsequent centuries. For details see S. Loffreda, “Capernaum — Jesus’ Own City,” Bible and Spade 10.1 (1981): 1-17.
Grk “him”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “they asked him about her.” It is clear from the context that they were concerned about her physical condition. The verb “to help” in the translation makes this explicit.

verses.zh: 耶稣站在她旁边，斥责那热病，热就退了。她立刻起来服事他们。
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] he stood over her, commanded[NOTE:2] the fever, and it left her. Immediately[NOTE:3] she got up and began to serve[NOTE:4] them.
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate the resultative nature of Jesus’ actions.

The language here (commanded) almost treats the illness as a personal force (see vv. 35, 41), but this is not the case. This healing shows Jesus’ power over sickness and should not be construed as an exorcism.tn Or “rebuked,” but “rebuke” implies strong disapproval, while the usage here involves more of a command with perhaps the implication of a threat (L&N 33.331).

The note that this happened immediately shows the speed and totality of the recovery.tn Grk “and immediately.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, δέ (de) has not been translated here. Instead a new sentence is started in the translation.
The imperfect verb has been translated ingressively.

verses.zh: 日落的时候，凡有病人的，不论害甚么病，都带到耶稣那里。耶稣按手在他们各人身上，医好他们。
verses.en: As the sun was setting, all those who had any relatives[NOTE:1] sick with various diseases brought them to Jesus.[NOTE:2] He placed[NOTE:3] his hands on every one of them and healed them.
notes: Grk “everyone, as many as had those being sick.” The use of εἶχον (eichon, “had”) suggests that the subject of the accusative participle ἀσθενοῦντας (asthenountas, “those being sick”) is not simply acquaintances, but rather relatives, perhaps immediate family, and certainly close friends.
Grk “him”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “laid.” The participle ἐπιτεθείς (epitetheis) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

verses.zh: 又有鬼从好些人身上出来，喊着说：「你是　神的儿子。」耶稣斥责他们，不许他们说话。因为他们知道他是基督。
verses.en: Demons also came out[NOTE:1] of many, crying out,[NOTE:2] “You are the Son of God!”[NOTE:3] But he rebuked[NOTE:4] them and would not allow them to speak[NOTE:5] because they knew that he was the Christ.[NOTE:6]
notes: Demons also came out. Note how Luke distinguishes healing from exorcism here, implying that the two are not identical.
Grk “crying out and saying.” The participle λέγοντα (legonta) is redundant in English and has not been translated here.

Most mss (A Q Θ Ψ 0102 ƒ1,13 M) read “the Christ, the Son of God.” But the earliest and best mss, along with several other witnesses (א B C D L W Ξ 33 579 700 1241 2542 lat sa), lack “the Christ” here. It is likely that later scribes wished to bring the demons’ confession in line with what Luke says they knew later in the verse.
Or “commanded,” but “rebuke” implies strong disapproval, which seems to be more in keeping with the context here (L&N 33.419).

Jesus would not allow the demons to speak because the time for such disclosure was not yet at hand, and such a revelation would have certainly been misunderstood by the people. In all likelihood, if the people had understood him early on to be the Son of God, or Messiah, they would have reduced his mission to one of political deliverance from Roman oppression (cf. John 6:15). Jesus wanted to avoid, as much as possible, any premature misunderstanding about who he was and what he was doing. However, at the end of his ministry, he did not deny such a title when the high priest asked him (22:66-71).

Note how Luke associates Son of God with Messiah (Christ) in this context, a regal connection with OT roots (Ps 2:7). Also, see the note on Christ in 2:11.tn Or “Messiah”; both “Christ” (Greek) and “Messiah” (Hebrew and Aramaic) mean “one who has been anointed.”

verses.zh: 天亮的时候，耶稣出来，走到旷野地方。众人去找他，到了他那里，要留住他，不要他离开他们。
verses.en: The next morning[NOTE:1] Jesus[NOTE:2] departed and went to a deserted place. Yet[NOTE:3] the crowds were seeking him, and they came to him and tried to keep him from leaving them.
notes: Grk “When it became day.”
Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Here καί (kai) has been translated as “yet” to indicate that the crowds still sought Jesus in spite of his withdrawal.

verses.zh: 但耶稣对他们说：「我也必须在别城传　神国的福音，因我奉差原是为此。」
verses.en: But Jesus[NOTE:1] said to them, “I must[NOTE:2] proclaim the good news of the kingdom[NOTE:3] of God to the other towns[NOTE:4] too, for that is what I was sent[NOTE:5] to do.”[NOTE:6]
notes: Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Here δεῖ (dei, “it is necessary”) indicates divine commission (cf. Luke 2:49).
The good news of the kingdom, the kingdom of the rule of God through the Messiah, is the topic of Jesus’ preaching.
Or “cities.”
Jesus was sent by God for this purpose. This is the language of divine commission.
Grk “because for this purpose I was sent.”

verses.zh: 于是耶稣在加利利的各会堂传道。
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] he continued to preach in the synagogues of Judea.[NOTE:2]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate the summarization.

Most mss (A D Θ Ψ ƒ13 33 M latt) have “of Galilee”; others, “of the Jews” (W). “Judea” (read by P75 א B Q 579 892 sa, and [with minor variation] C L ƒ1 1241) is probably the earlier reading since it is both the harder reading and supported by the best witnesses. “Galilee” is an assimilation to Mark 1:39 and Matt 4:23.
